plate.subject: masons and mourners at a rebuilt wall

paragraphs.text: The Second Age lasted 2,133 years, the longest of the ages of Aoaz. It began after Volgan’s defeat at Dardan and Elzon’s repulse of the Grand Alliance from the Ember Lands. It ended in 2A 2133, when Elzon took Aenor and set up his order, and the Third Age began.

It has three names. The Age of Rebuilding is what the survivors meant to do. The Age of Long Grief and the Dark Age are what later generations remember, for wars, plagues, raids, corruption and disasters of the spirit world went on for generation after generation. All three are used in different chronicles.

sources.section: XI. The end of the Second Age

paragraphs.text: Yet it was not one long collapse. Men learned better farming, ways to prevent famine, the treatment of plagues, the order of armies and the building of strong walls. These things carried later generations through the Third Age and into the long peace of the Fourth.

sources.section: New canonical refinements: the long but creative Second Age

paragraphs.text: King Edran ruled the first years of rebuilding and died of disease. Orcs and goblins fought on for Volgan, and the Dark Lands fell back into turmoil. Demons came through opened gates to raid Aenor. Elzon, patient and immortal, worked against every recovery, freed Volgan’s spirit from the Void, and drew on old magic of Zol, the first sign of that Old God’s stirring. In the end Elzon and Volgan won.

The scholars of Parim divide the age into seven periods: the Long Mourning (2A 1 to 240), the Wars of the Remnants (241 to 660), the Hard Centuries (661 to 1150), the Open Gates (1151 to 1550), and, in the last six centuries of the age, the Return, the War from Within and the Fallen Crown. The years of Edran’s death and of Volgan’s return are not known.
paragraphs.note: The seven periods and their year bands are proposed; the end year and the open dates are established.

sources.section: XIII. Chronological sequence and dating constraints
XV. Canonical 2,133-year calendar and proposed internal periods

paragraphs.text: The lesson the scholars draw is that the world lost over many generations. Good kings and brave people could not undo the weight of destruction, mistrust between peoples, disease, the hunger of powers beyond men, and Elzon’s patience. That is why the restoration of the Fourth Age is remembered as it is.

sources.section: XI. The end of the Second Age

plate.subject: a king's bier in a half-rebuilt hall, empty chairs at a council table

paragraphs.text: The last armies came back from the Ember Lands with little to celebrate. They had broken Volgan at Dardan but had not destroyed his kingdom. Villages across Aenor had lost whole generations, fields lay untended, roads had become burial grounds, and refugees crowded into cities that could barely feed them. The dead could not all be named or buried.

sources.section: II. The age that followed victory

paragraphs.text: King Edran inherited a kingdom still worth saving. He restored granaries, bridges, mills and walls, and the old roads from the Middle Lands to the coast. His first laws sent soldiers back to the land and stopped the great nobles from taking abandoned farms for themselves. His scribes went into the ruined provinces to keep the Registers of the Lost, recording the dead, finding the missing and settling inheritances, so that grieving families had proof their own had lived.

sources.section: II. The age that followed victory

paragraphs.text: The Grand Alliance did not vanish at once, but the failed invasion had soured it. The Gala elves mourned their dead, and the elves of the Magical Lands no longer trusted every Aenoran call for soldiers. The West Lands remembered Aenor’s old conquests, and the rulers of the east and north had their own frontiers to guard. No king could summon a single army by decree any more. That loss of unity was the first gift the victory left to Elzon.

sources.section: II. The age that followed victory

paragraphs.text: The former allies met once more in the Council of the Empty Chairs, named for the seats left vacant for commanders who died at Dardan or in the failed invasion. The king wanted a common army on the border of the Ember Lands. Some elven envoys offered scouts and healers but refused another invasion. The western rulers asked that Aenor first give up its disputed claims. No settlement came of it, though aid, trade and friendships went on.

sources.section: Proposed episode: the Council of the Empty Chairs

paragraphs.text: Edran, the great king of the Grand Alliance, guided the rebuilding of the early Second Age and at last died of disease. It is not known in what year he died, at what age, or of what illness. His death was one episode in a long line of successions and renewals, and Aenor did not fall with him.

Centuries later the Registers of the Lost carried a darker meaning. The necromancers of Elzon learned to use the names and places of the dead to find their graves. The registers did not make necromancy; they only became knowledge in the hands of those who already had it.

sources.section: II. The age that followed victory

paragraphs.text: Many orcs and goblins went on fighting for Volgan long after his banishment, and the independent Dark Lands fell back into turmoil. Elzon, an immortal Great Spirit, Volgan’s servant and the Great Necromancer, had survived the First Age. He set himself to hinder Aenor’s recovery with raids, alliances and ever wider networks of servants.

A Great Spirit can think in centuries and rebuild after defeats that would end a mortal captain. At first Elzon did not march on Aenor; his forces were too scattered to repeat Volgan’s invasion. He built instead a second kingdom without borders. Its roads were smugglers’ paths, its forts were hidden shrines and cavern strongholds, and its servants worked inside foreign courts.

sources.section: III. Elzon, the enemy who remained

paragraphs.text: The scholars call that kingdom the Ash Networks: a loose band of orc warbands, goblin clans, surviving dark captains, spies, thieves, necromancers, men who served him in secret and scattered agents of the demons. Their loyalty varied. Some worshipped Volgan, some feared Elzon, some wanted land or wealth, and some had lost any place in a world at peace.

Elzon seldom struck the same way twice. One year frontier bridges burned; in another a port governor vanished and the grain ships went astray; elsewhere a failed rising drove refugees into lands that could not feed them. His worst work was the death of trust. Aenoran armies treated suspected traitors as enemies, their reprisals filled his ranks, and provincial nobles raised their own garrisons and claimed the powers of the crown.

The Dark Lands were never one realm. Independent rulers, monster peoples, corrupted courts and rival warlords fought for power there; some served Elzon, and others fought him because they remembered Volgan’s grip. Orcs and goblins serve no single master by nature. In the War of the Black Roads his followers tried to seize the roads through the Dark Lands, and a free confederation stood against them.
Aenor helped that confederation for a time, until its leaders asked for more than the king could give. So the Dark Lands stayed divided between hostile, watchful and independent powers.

plate.subject: healers and granaries in a plague-year town

paragraphs.text: Wars, famine, disease, raids and corruption kept the Second Age from any long, unbroken recovery after Dardan, and so it is remembered as the Dark Age and the Age of Long Grief. Yet it was not all suffering. Aenor and other lands made great progress in the arts of war, in the treatment and cure of disease, in farming and in the prevention of famine. These gains kept later generations alive and helped Aenor recover in the Fourth Age.

Sickness spread again and again through crowded cities, refugee camps, ruined farmland and trade roads. Some plagues rose from ordinary hardship and poor living. Others came of sorcery, corrupted places, or creatures from broken realms. Even the scholars of the time could seldom tell which was which.

sources.section: IV. The years of sickness and open gates

paragraphs.text: The Grey Breath swept the crowded winter settlements after failed harvests; some rulers blamed demons, but no proof of it survives. The Lantern Blight haunted the lands near unstable gates, where sleep was broken, fires burned strangely and the dead seemed to stand among their families. Grave Fever was the name people gave to the outbreaks around mass graves and old battlefields, which Elzon’s agents sometimes used.

sources.section: IV. The years of sickness and open gates

paragraphs.text: Farmers learned to rotate their crops, to grow plants that endured drought, to dig irrigation canals, to keep seed in reserve and to build better stores, and villages agreed common rules for the harvest. Healers became specialists. They sought cleaner water, kept the sick of certain fevers apart, made remedies from the plants of each region and shared their records of the sick. Not every plague was magic, and not every cure a miracle.

Soldiers learned to build walls in layers and to defend against siege, to move supply in ordered columns, to keep messengers, roads and reserves, and to make weapons that could stop fast raids or stand against the dead. Rulers who distrusted each other still agreed to open roads and trade grain, and set up neutral hospitals in time of war. These were the work of generations of engineers, farmers, healers and soldiers.

Suffering also bred new faiths, desperate bargains and false prophets. The king’s servants tried to keep the old laws, while local governors more and more made bargains with powers they barely understood.

sources.section: IV. The years of sickness and open gates

plate.subject: a burning portal inside a border fort

paragraphs.text: The Nether lies in the south of the Ember Lands. It is the seat of the King of Demons, whose name no chronicle of men gives. His pacts bind the living; the souls of the dead remain Zol’s. The Nether is not the Void, where Volgan was banished, nor the Abyss, where Roka and his necklace are found.

Agon was a demon active in the Second Age, and he belonged to the Nether. It is not known what rank he held, whom he served, or how he stood to the King of Demons, and no chronicle shows that he was that king.

In the Second Age gates opened across parts of Aoaz, and demons came through them to raid Aenor and other peoples. Some gates were opened on purpose by cults or by powerful demons; others may have been wounds in the old boundaries left by earlier wars. The demons struck settlements, carried off goods and captives, bargained with frightened rulers and fought one another for influence.
paragraphs.note: The gates and the raids are established; the causes of the gates and the kinds of raid are proposed.

paragraphs.text: Not all of these raids were Elzon’s doing. The demons of the Nether had their own purposes. Some worked with him, some fought him, and others simply took Aenor’s weakness as their chance. Demons were never one realm, and not all of them served Volgan.
paragraphs.note: That demons need not serve Volgan or act as one realm is established; their dealings with Elzon are proposed.

paragraphs.text: At the Burning Gate of Nezer a portal opened inside a contested border stronghold. The human garrison, an elven relief company and a band of independent soldiers of the dark country fought side by side and closed it. The royal historians forgot their victory, because the three peoples took up their quarrels again within a generation. The scholars keep it as proof that men and other peoples could still stand together.

Rumours that Volgan still lived spread long before most men knew that Elzon meant to bring him back. Priests disagreed about the Void. Veterans swore they had felt his presence after Dardan. Prophets spoke of a darkness that had not finished its work.

sources.section: V. The prophecies of the return

paragraphs.text: Some warnings rose from true disturbances in the world of spirits. Others were fear, invention, or lies spread on purpose by Elzon’s agents. That Volgan did return does not make every prophecy true.

sources.section: V. The prophecies of the return

paragraphs.text: One prophecy survives in many copies: “The king cast out shall return without a crown. His servant shall open what the victors closed, and the graves of men shall become his gates.” Its words may have been set down long before the return, changed in translation, or made after the event by chroniclers. The temples still dispute it.

sources.section: V. The prophecies of the return

paragraphs.text: A small order of mortals and spirits, the Watchers of Dardan, kept guard over the ruined field where the Great Spirits had banished Volgan. They found that the signs of the old binding had begun to fail. A few surviving spirits of the alliance knew the danger, but the kingdoms agreed too little to raise a new alliance.

sources.section: Proposed episode: the Watchers of Dardan

plate.subject: a storm gathering into a shape over red desert

paragraphs.text: In the Second Age the Great Necromancer Elzon freed his master from the Void. Volgan’s soul, or his spiritual presence, came back to Aoaz. The return was real, not a false prophecy. But Volgan needed time to win back the power stripped from him at Dardan, and he gave Elzon far greater freedom to act.

Volgan had been banished at Dardan, not destroyed, and Elzon broke through only after centuries of work. Elzon could not force the Void open by strength. He studied the scar the banishment had left, sought out those who had witnessed it, gathered relics touched by the binding and searched the dormant passages beneath the Ember Lands. He destroyed several failed attempts before he found a way.
paragraphs.note: The centuries of work are established in outline; the method is proposed.

paragraphs.text: The scholars say the rite needed three things: a trace of Volgan’s spirit kept in the Ember Lands, a threshold weakened through flaws in the old binding, and ancient death-magic of Zol, strong enough to reach across a boundary no ordinary sorcery can cross. The breach led to the Void. It was no gate of the Nether, and it did not touch the Abyss.

The cost was immense. Several of Elzon’s oldest strongholds were consumed, captains loyal to him were sacrificed or destroyed, and he could not easily work the rite again. He did it in secret, because every rival power, some demons among them, would have sought to seize its result.

What returned was presence, not strength. Volgan’s mind and will could act in Aoaz again and slowly regain influence, but the host he had lost did not come back to him. The war against Aenor was now Elzon’s to make. He was no longer only the keeper of the Ember Lands; he raised his own networks, led his own wars, dealt with spirits and held conquered lands under his own order, while he stayed loyal to Volgan.
paragraphs.note: The return of presence without full strength and Elzon’s greater freedom are established; the forms that freedom took are proposed.

paragraphs.text: It is not known how Elzon reached Zol’s magic or what it cost him, where the rite was done, in what form Volgan first showed himself again, or why the spirits who had bound him could not seal the way once more. No chronicle shows that Zol allowed it, or that he and Elzon were allies.

plate.subject: a still black sea and silent graves at night

paragraphs.text: Zol came to Aoaz long before Aen or Volgan. He is the only Old God in Aoaz, and the God of Death, and his domain is Zol’s Mistake in the north. His power is immense, but the Fading and the nature of Aoaz’s magic hold him back. He cannot take a body and conquer a kingdom.

sources.section: VII. The first stirring of Zol

paragraphs.text: Through the early ages Zol lay mostly dormant. The Second Age is when his presence first became plain to others, when Elzon drew on his old magic. That does not mean Zol had woken from sleep or had lost his power before. It means that the peoples of Aoaz met a sign of his influence on a scale they had never known.

sources.section: VII. The first stirring of Zol

paragraphs.text: In the far north there were nights when every sound stopped around the ancient graves, and the sea about Zol’s Mistake lay unnaturally still. In distant lands necromancers felt a presence behind their common rites, and a few dreamers spoke of an absence like a face, watching from beyond the living world. No army ever saw Zol on a battlefield.

sources.section: VII. The first stirring of Zol

paragraphs.text: No chronicle tells whether Elzon stole Zol’s ancient workings, bargained for them, copied them or was given them. None shows that Elzon served Zol, that Zol favoured Volgan, or that the Old God sought the conquest of Aenor.

sources.section: VII. The first stirring of Zol

paragraphs.text: The scholars keep one distinction above all. Elzon controls and raises the dead by sorcery. Zol is the Old God of Death itself. However great Elzon’s necromancy, it never raised him to Zol’s height.

sources.section: VII. The first stirring of Zol

plate.subject: an elven gate closed against smoke on the horizon

paragraphs.text: In the late First Age the elves, Lorien and his Gala host among them, helped the Grand Alliance defeat Volgan at Dardan. Afterwards King Edran insisted on an attempt to conquer the Ember Lands, against the elves’ opposition. Elzon’s defenders drove the expedition back and inflicted enormous losses, the elves’ among them.

That mistake destroyed the trust that another Grand Alliance would have needed. In the Second Age, when Elzon invaded Aenor, the elven kingdoms did not send armies to help men. The refusal was a lasting fruit of Edran’s decision, and no new alliance was made in the last invasion.

Independent elven communities defended their own Magical Lands. That was not the same as renewing an alliance to save the human crown. Single travellers, healers and others cooperated across the races, but no elven host ever marched to free the crown of men.

sources.section: New canonical refinements: the long but creative Second Age

paragraphs.text: In the Third Age the elves of the Magical Lands fought Elzon to defend their own unconquered lands. That fits their earlier refusal.

entries.title: The War of the Hollow Crown
entries.subtitle: Second Age · War

plate.subject: a royal host facing the risen dead before a capital

paragraphs.text: When Elzon at last opened his final wars, Aenor had already been fighting for generations. Exhausted hereditary houses ruled several provinces, some regions obeyed the crown in name but sent nothing to its army, and the West Lands would not accept a new Aenoran supremacy. Elzon’s war came from within and from every side at once, and many who fought in it never saw that their struggles were one.
paragraphs.note: A war from within and from many sides is established; the condition of the provinces is proposed.

paragraphs.text: First came the Thousand Small Wars: his agents armed rival noble houses, monster lords and rebel governors, and raids drew the royal armies off the great roads. Then the Broken Oaths: corrupted leaders and forged letters set men, elves and dwarves against one another, some over true grievances of the First Age, some by sorcery or fraud, until alliances fell apart with neither side sure why.

sources.section: Proposed sequence of the great unraveling

paragraphs.text: Then the Opening of the Passes: orc and goblin armies came through lands thought safe, some down from the Dark Lands and some up from deep below. Last came the March of the Unburied. Elzon took the field in full power and raised the dead from battlefields, graveyards, abandoned forts and roadsides, and Aenor’s soldiers saw their own dead kin and comrades among his ranks.
paragraphs.note: That Elzon took the field and raised Aenor’s fallen is established; the names and order of the stages are proposed.

sources.section: Proposed sequence of the great unraveling

paragraphs.text: The last war is called the War of the Hollow Crown. Raids and revolt cut off two great grain provinces, and the king had to choose between the frontier and feeding the capital, while Elzon struck at the supply columns, not the strongest walls. Then his necromancers took the burial roads from the old battlefields to the cities, and an army the crown thought destroyed rose again farther inland.

sources.section: Proposed final campaign: the War of the Hollow Crown

paragraphs.text: The North Lands sent help, too late and too few. The elven kingdoms sent no army, remembering Edran’s folly, and guarded their own lands. The western kingdoms refused the summons or fought their own wars at sea; they had their own enemies. Near the approaches to the capital the last royal host met Elzon’s dead, and its own fallen rose against it. Companies that would not leave their wounded were surrounded.
paragraphs.note: The elven refusal is established; the rest of the account is proposed.

sources.section: Proposed final campaign: the War of the Hollow Crown

paragraphs.text: Aenor did not fall in one great battle. Every defeat cost it soldiers and veterans, and part of those same losses passed to Elzon. The scholars hold that his dead needed remains within reach, a binding of name, mark or place, and power enough to hold them, and men learned to guard their graves, carry off their fallen and break the shrines that sustained his hosts. No defence was ever sure.

plate.subject: pale banners raised over a fallen capital

paragraphs.text: At the close of the Second Age, in 2A 2133, Elzon won his war against Aenor, seized the kingdom and set up his order. Volgan had returned from the Void, and the two prevailed together. The conquest began the Third Age.

Elzon entered the royal city after its defence had collapsed. No chronicle tells the name of the last free king or what became of the royal line, and the scholars do not agree whether the royal city of that age was Parim, the seat of the Fourth Age. They record the conquest simply as the Fall of Aenor.
paragraphs.note: Elzon’s entry after the collapse is proposed; the open questions are established.

sources.section: Proposed final campaign: the War of the Hollow Crown

paragraphs.text: Not every subject was killed. Elzon gained more from farms, roads, craftsmen and frightened but living officials. His order held the land with garrisons of the dead, necromantic officers, mortal administrators who submitted, and client rulers bound to give labour, food, news and bodies. Pockets of human resistance, free elves, dwarves and other peoples remained.

Men called the new rule Elzon’s Order. Later historians call it the Pale Regency, for Elzon ruled in the name of a master who had returned but had not recovered his old greatness. He ruled with the freedom that Volgan had given him.
paragraphs.note: Elzon’s Order is established; the name the Pale Regency is proposed.

paragraphs.text: A royal archivist, Arelon, the Keeper of the Last Seal, carried fragments of Aenor’s oldest genealogies and laws out of the fallen city. He did not save the royal treasures. He saved the records that named the descendants of Aen and the rights of the crown.

sources.section: Proposed survivor: the Keeper of the Last Seal

paragraphs.text: So the age ended. The old capital was lost, Elzon’s Order stood in the crown’s place, and Volgan’s spirit was back in Aoaz. The Nether still sent its raids and its rival demonic interests, and men knew that Zol’s presence had been felt, though not what part he had played.

sources.section: XI. The end of the Second Age

entries.title: The Night of a Thousand Oaths
entries.subtitle: Second Age · Secret

paragraphs.text: Afrit grew ever more powerful through the Second Age, and his ascension near its end was one of the age’s defining events. He had used the First Age war to destroy a rival, and he used the ruin that followed to gain worship, influence and power by cults, contracts, bargains, favours and corruption. He stayed independent of Elzon and of Volgan.

The age gave him all he needed: men feared the Nether, noble houses quarrelled, priests could not halt disease, and the bereaved would bargain with any power that promised safety. In ruined towns his hidden followers ran the Houses of Refuge, giving grain, medicine, shelter and protection, and most who took them never learned whose gifts they were. Each small debt could be passed from a family to a guild, a temple or a lord.

On the Night of a Thousand Oaths, priests and rulers bound by separate compacts found that their obligations had become one web. Worshippers in many lands bound themselves under the same name without knowing whom they served, and through that web Afrit could cast his influence at a scale never seen. No chronicle fixes the night’s date in the last years of the age.

sources.section: The ascension near the end of the Second Age

paragraphs.text: The ascension did not make Afrit a New God, and what order of being it raised him to is not known. It gave him neither Roka’s Necklace of the Abyss, which he took only in the Fourth Age, nor Aenor’s crown. Elzon took the kingdom he had hoped to inherit, and so the two became rivals.
paragraphs.note: The limits are established; the rivalry over the crown is proposed.

sources.section: The ascension near the end of the Second Age

paragraphs.text: His public godhood came later. Near the end of the Third Age he was acclaimed a New God for saving the world from Elzon, and the people worshipped him as their Deliverer. Whether he truly belongs to the divine order the Holy Seven made is not known.

sources.section: His later recognition as a New God
